messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Musa was a 47-year-old single African man who worked as a park ranger, a job that once meant long days on foot, checking trails, speaking with visitors, and knowing the land by smell, sound, and the angle of light through the trees. Years earlier, while working as a civilian guide in a war zone in East Africa, he had been caught in an attack near a wooded outpost when fighting spread unexpectedly through the area. He remembered smoke rising among the trees, the sudden flash of fire in dry brush, shouted orders from armed men in military uniforms, and the sickening pause when a group he had been helping was struck and he survived while others did not. What stayed with him most was not only the violence itself but the way he had acted to keep moving and stay alive, actions he later judged as shameful and against the kind of man he believed himself to be.

In the months after that event, Musa found that even small reminders pulled him back into the same dread. A supervisor’s criticism at work could hit him like danger, because being corrected now felt less like feedback than the first sign that something terrible was about to happen. If a fire pit was lit at a campground or he saw flames from a controlled burn, his body tightened immediately, and if he walked in a forest that resembled the place where the attack happened, the whole day could collapse into alarm. Those moments left him unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, and he began sleeping badly, lying awake listening for sounds he could not trust. When something at work took longer than expected, he assumed something bad was happening on the trail or that a crisis had begun out of sight. The same sights and situations also drove him deeper into himself: he cut off contact with friends and family, stopped answering calls, and avoided any setting where he might see military or police uniforms or weapons, because those images seemed to belong to the world that had swallowed the people he could not save.

Musa had come to believe that surviving meant something was wrong with him. He felt guilty for being alive when others did not make it out, and that guilt carried a harsh sense that he had violated his own values in the way he had tried to preserve himself. He described feeling isolated and set apart from other people, as if his life had split off from theirs at the moment of the attack. When he was criticized, or when he found himself back among trees and brush that looked too much like the original place, those appraisals surged again: he was certain that he had failed the dead, that he no longer belonged among ordinary people, and that the man he had been before the war was gone. The more he judged himself in this way, the more on edge he became, and the more he braced for danger.

That constant strain shaped the way he moved through his days. He drank alcohol and took medication or drugs to blunt the tension and force himself through evenings when his thoughts would not settle. But the short-lived relief left him more withdrawn and more vulnerable to the very reminders he was trying to outrun. After drinking, he often woke with his heart racing and his sleep even more broken, and the fatigue made him quicker to see threat in delays, criticism, or a patch of woodland that resembled the site of the attack. Because he had isolated so completely, he spent less time with people who might have helped challenge these fears; instead, the silence around him made his guilt and sense of separation grow stronger, which in turn made the world feel more dangerous. At the park, he started taking different routes to avoid areas where visitors lit fires or where ranger vehicles and uniforms would remind him of armed men, and the effort of avoiding those cues kept the event close in his mind. The more he arranged his life around not seeing, not hearing, and not being reminded, the more ordinary surroundings seemed loaded with threat, and the more easily his thoughts turned back to what had happened and what he believed it said about him.

By the time Musa sought help, he was exhausted by sleeping poorly, unable to relax even in his own home, and increasingly afraid that his life had narrowed to a series of cautions and withdrawals. He came because he could no longer carry the guilt and the constant sense that something bad was about to happen, and because he feared that if this continued he would lose the last pieces of himself that still felt loyal to who he believed he was. What he hoped for, though he said it carefully, was to sleep again, to walk the trails without feeling hunted by fire, criticism, and trees, and to find a way to be around people without feeling cut off from them.
